zh.principle:
**定理**：Rompel 定理（OWF Implies Digital Signatures）。### 单向函数足够造签名

Rompel 定理：安全数字签名存在，当且仅当单向函数存在。必要性直接：签名方案本身可导出单向函数（例如把公钥或消息映射成难以求逆的串）；难点是充分性：只给一个任意 OWF，如何造出抗自适应选择消息伪造的签名。### 三层构造

1.OWF → UOWHF。通用单向哈希函数（UOWHF）压缩长消息，且给定一个原像后难以找到同像的另一原像。Rompel 证明任意 OWF 都能构造 UOWHF。2.UOWHF → 一次性签名。Lamport 一次性签名把消息每一位映射到两个秘密串；公钥是它们的散列。签名揭示每位对应的一个秘密串，验证重新散列。3.一次性签名 → 多次签名。Merkle 树把 N 个一次性公钥作为叶子，根作为总公钥；每次签名附上叶子公钥、一次性签名和到根的路径。### Lamport 的代数

私钥 s_{i,b}←{0,1}^n，公钥 pk_{i,b}=H(s_{i,b})。消息 m 的签名是 (s_{1,m_1},…,s_{n,m_n})。验证：对每个 i 计算 H(s_{i,m_i}) 并与 pk_{i,m_i} 比较。同一密钥签两条不同消息，会在某个不同位泄漏两个原像，攻击者可伪造第三条消息。
zh.why:
公钥加密需要陷门，签名却不需要：Rompel 说明签名可以只建立在 OWF 上。它把 Lamport 的一次性签名、Merkle 的树和 Naor–Yung 的 UOWHF 组合成一个完整的 EUF-CMA 方案。### 对今天的影响

哈希签名（XMSS、LMS、SPHINCS+）都沿着“一次性签名 + 树”这条路。Rompel 的定理给出理论保证：即使没有 RSA/ECC，只要有 OWF，就能签名；后量子时代这尤其重要。
zh.used: - 理论：证明 OWF 是签名的充分必要条件；为哈希签名提供归约骨架。- 工程：Lamport/Merkle 的一次性签名与树结构用于代码签名、区块链、后量子签名候选；实际方案优化了密钥/签名尺寸和状态管理。- 读法：先看一次性签名是否只用一次，再看树是否覆盖所有叶子，最后看 UOWHF 是否抗同像。Rompel 的原始构造是渐近的；它不是 ECDSA 的替代品，而是“没有数论假设也能签名”的存在性证明。
zh.broken: 1.效率极低。Lamport 公钥含 2n 个散列，签名为 n 个秘密串；Merkle 树再加 log N 个节点。实际部署需要优化或换用更紧凑的哈希签名。2.有状态。Merkle 树签名必须记录已用叶子；重复使用叶子会破坏一次性安全性。无状态方案（如 SPHINCS+）用不同的树/随机化来避免状态。3.UOWHF 构造复杂。Rompel 的证明很长，且原会议论文的若干论证后来被指出有错误；Katz–Koo 2005 才给出完整重写。不能把“OWF→UOWHF”当成一行代码。4.安全归约损失。树高、消息长度与哈希族参数都会进入界；具体参数要按方案的安全目标计算。5.不是公钥加密。OWF 足以签名，但不足以构造公钥加密；后者仍需陷门。“哈希签名因此绝对安全”不成立。它依赖 OWF/哈希的抗碰撞或抗第二原像假设，并依赖一次性密钥不被重用；实现错误仍会破坏安全。
zh.history:
Lamport 1979 提出一次性签名；Merkle 1979 提出用树把一次性签名扩展为多次签名；Naor–Yung 1989 用 UOWHF 构造签名。Rompel 1990 在 STOC 上证明任意 OWF 都能构造 UOWHF，从而完成 OWF→签名的链条。### 后续与修正

Rompel 的会议论文影响很大，但若干证明细节长期没有完整发表；Katz 与 Koo 在 2005 年给出完整重写，并指出原论文中的一些错误。哈希签名后来进入 NIST 后量子标准进程（SPHINCS+ 等），这条路线在今天比 1990 年更现实。

en.principle:
**Theorem**: OWF Implies Digital Signatures (Rompel 定理). ### One-way functions suffice for signatures

Rompel’s theorem: secure digital signatures exist if and only if one-way functions exist. Necessity is direct: a signature scheme itself yields a one-way function (for example, mapping a public key or message to a hard-to-invert string). The hard direction is sufficiency: given only an arbitrary OWF, construct a signature secure against adaptive chosen-message forgery. ### Three construction layers

1. OWF → UOWHF. A universal one-way hash function (UOWHF) compresses long messages and makes it hard, given one preimage, to find a different preimage of the same value. Rompel proved that any OWF constructs a UOWHF. UOWHF → one-time signature. The Lamport one-time signature maps each message bit to two secret strings; the public key consists of their hashes. A signature reveals one secret string per bit, and verification re-hashes. One-time signature → many signatures. A Merkle tree puts N one-time public keys at the leaves and the root as the overall public key; each signature carries the leaf key, the one-time signature and the path to the root. ### Lamport’s algebra

Private key s_{i,b}←{0,1}^n, public key pk_{i,b}=H(s_{i,b}). A signature on m is (s_{1,m_1},…,s_{n,m_n}). Verification hashes each revealed string and compares it with pk_{i,m_i}. Signing two different messages under one key leaks both preimages at some differing bit, letting an attacker forge a third message.
en.why:
Public-key encryption needs a trapdoor; signatures do not: Rompel showed signatures can rest on OWF alone. He combined Lamport’s one-time signature, Merkle’s tree and the Naor–Yung UOWHF into a complete EUF-CMA scheme.

Hash-based signatures (XMSS, LMS, SPHINCS+) all follow the “one-time signature + tree” path. Rompel’s theorem gives a theoretical guarantee: even without RSA/ECC, an OWF suffices for signatures; in the post-quantum era this matters even more.
en.used:
- Theory: proves OWF is necessary and sufficient for signatures; supplies the reduction skeleton for hash-based signatures. - Engineering: Lamport/Merkle one-time signatures and trees are used in code signing, blockchains and post-quantum signature candidates; practical schemes optimize key/signature size and state management. - Reading: check that a one-time signature is used once, the tree covers all leaves, and the UOWHF resists target collisions.

Rompel’s original construction is asymptotic; it is not a replacement for ECDSA, but an existence proof that signatures need no number-theoretic assumption.
en.broken:
1. Very inefficient. A Lamport public key contains 2n hashes and a signature contains n secret strings; a Merkle tree adds log N nodes. Deployment needs optimization or a more compact hash signature. 2. Stateful. A Merkle-tree signer must record used leaves; reusing a leaf breaks one-time security. Stateless schemes (such as SPHINCS+) use different trees/randomization to avoid state. 3. The UOWHF construction is complex. Rompel’s proof was long, and several arguments in the original conference paper were later found flawed; Katz–Koo 2005 gave a complete rewrite. “OWF→UOWHF” is not one line of code. 4. Reduction loss. Tree height, message length and hash-family parameters enter the bound; concrete parameters must be computed for the scheme’s security target. 5. It is not public-key encryption. OWF suffices for signatures but not for public-key encryption; the latter still needs a trapdoor.

“Hash signatures are therefore absolutely secure” is false. They rely on OWF/hash collision or second-preimage assumptions and on one-time keys never being reused; implementation errors can still break security.
en.history:
Lamport proposed one-time signatures in 1979; Merkle proposed extending them to many messages with a tree in 1979; Naor–Yung 1989 built signatures from UOWHFs. Rompel 1990 at STOC proved that any OWF constructs a UOWHF, completing the OWF→signature chain.

Rompel’s conference paper was influential, but several proof details were never fully published; Katz and Koo gave a complete rewrite in 2005 and noted errors in the original. Hash-based signatures later entered the NIST post-quantum process (SPHINCS+ and others); the route is more realistic today than in 1990.
